questions.question: Which leading bit identified historical Class A addressing?
questions.explanation: The first bit of a historical Class A address was zero.

questions.question: Before CIDR, which default mask was associated with an address beginning 150.20?
questions.explanation: First octet 150 falls into the old Class B range, whose default was /16.

questions.question: An archival addressing plan labels 198.18.4.0 as Class C. Which default prefix did that classification imply?
questions.explanation: Historical Class C uses leading bits 110 and a /24 classful boundary.

questions.question: A legacy reference labels 233.1.1.1 as Class D. What was this range used for?

options.B: Ordinary unicast networks with a /24 mask
options.D: Limited broadcast on the local LAN

questions.explanation: Class D addresses have leading bits 1110 and identify multicast groups.

questions.question: Which leading pattern identifies the historical Class E block?
questions.explanation: The 240.0.0.0/4 range starts with 1111 and was historically reserved. It contains special cases such as limited broadcast.

questions.question: A test program binds to 127.5.4.3. What is the intended address scope?

options.B: A private subnet routable across a site

questions.question: Which address identifies the subnet containing 203.0.113.183/26?
questions.explanation: A /26 block containing .183 starts at .128, where all six host bits are zero.

questions.question: A routing table explicitly lists 192.0.2.0/26. Which statement describes the prefix?

options.A: It excludes the lower half of the /24
options.C: It represents the .0 through .63 address block
options.D: It represents all addresses in 192.0.2.0/24 by historical class

questions.explanation: Modern forwarding uses the supplied prefix, whose six host bits describe 64 addresses.

questions.question: Which address is reserved as directed broadcast within 172.22.112.0/20?
questions.explanation: The third octet spans 112–127, and all host bits are ones at 172.22.127.255.

questions.question: A legacy Class A network includes first octet 11. Which fact decides whether 11.20.1.1 is RFC 1918 private today?

options.A: Whether its current mask is longer than /8
options.B: Whether the address falls in one of the listed RFC 1918 prefixes
options.C: Whether the address historically had a /8 mask
options.D: Whether its first octet is less than 127

questions.explanation: Private status follows specific ranges. 11.20.1.1 falls outside all three.
